en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun, *Jizhuan lunben*, Fascicle Twenty-seven.
The preceding section explaining the first two of the five Buddha-contemplations is now complete. Below follows the third: the causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Contemplation.
Within this, there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Regarding the question, the nature of the conditions refers to the four conditions.
Dependent origination consists of the twelve links of dependent origination.

In the explanation, it first clarifies that by investigating the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three periods of time through four principles, one realizes that there are only phenomena and no agent or experiencer.
The latter section clarifies the purification of the mind through contemplation of delusion (*moha*).
This first part contains two sections.
First, regarding the three periods of time, one perceives only formations (*saṃskāra*), only phenomena (*dharma*), only events (*vastu*), only causes (*hetu*), and only results (*phala*).
Subsequently, one investigates by means of the four principles:
because of the dependence upon ignorance and so forth, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth;
ignorance possesses only the functional activity of producing volitional formations.
Up to and including birth, which through its conventional function gives rise to old age and death;

there is scriptural authority (*āgama*) stating that dependent origination exists, and there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consisting of the knowledge of the origin of suffering that realizes it;
and against opposing arguments, there is inference (*anumāna*).
Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature of phenomena such as ignorance being the condition for volitional formations is *dharmatā*;
this is not dependent upon an agent or an experiencer.

In this context, there are only the various phenomena such as ignorance that are capable of inducing phenomena such as volitional formations; this is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The degree to which ignorance and the other factors serve as conditions for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth is precisely their nature as conditions.

In the fourth section, the "Contemplation of the Differentiation of the Elements," there is first a detailed explanation of the distinctions between the characteristics and natures of the six elements.

Second, regarding the explanation of the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*) following the various types of conceit (*mānacarita*): by reflecting upon the distinctions among the elements (*dhātu*), the mind of conceit attains purification.
Within this section, first, the six names are enumerated.
The detailed explanation of the six elements consists of six sections.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
the contemplation of the eighteen elements is called the "contemplation of the analysis of elements" (*dhātuprabhedabhāvanā*).
Regarding what these six elements explained here are:
Jiji states that these six elements are sufficient to encompass both the desire realm and the form realm.
Although earth is not limited to these eighteen elements, there exists this "earth-element" [within them].
That which is said to be "that which is comprised of internal, distinct solidity within this body" refers to that which is comprised of hardness as being earth.
The internal body, sense organs, and objects comprised within this earth element are appropriated by the ālayavijñāna;
now, since this earth element is intimately attached to those appropriated organs and objects,
this internal earth element is likewise appropriated by the ālayavijñāna.
Therefore, it is said that they are "intimately attached" and "appropriated.
The same principle applies to the water and other elements below.
Regarding the external earth element, it is said to be "neither intimately attached nor appropriated."

If the internal earth element is closely attached to its basis and resides proximately within the foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), such that it possesses the capacity for appropriation (*upādāna*),
the external earth element does not.
This is because external fire can burn villages, their constituent parts, and so forth.
Jingyun: Sometimes he causes an entire village to be burned, or he causes a portion of a village to be burned;
hence it is said, "or a village, or a part of a village," and so forth.
The subsequent commentary states:
"Alternatively, it refers to burning a village or the area outside the village,
such as places where refuse is discarded."
As clarified in the Vinaya,
regarding the internal wind element such as the "wind of lying on one's side" and so forth,
Jing says:
There are those afflicted with wind-disorders who can only lie on their backs with their sides up; this is called "lying on the spine" wind-disorder (*pṛṣṭhaśayana-vāta*).
Or there are those afflicted with wind-disorders whose bodily ailments are like being cut by small or large knives, and also like being pierced by needles.
There are those who, when afflicted by wind-disorders, develop black spots on their faces,
each resembling a *pi-pa-lo* (bimba) fruit.
Ji says:
Regarding the "wind that causes side-lying" and so forth:
this wind resides between the sides and enables such actions as lying down.
There is also a wind, like a small dagger, which is capable of injuring a person.
Regarding the *pippala* wind:
it is explained in the same manner as the *chāyā* [wind].
Furthermore, it is explained that *pippala* refers to the food consumed by humans.
This wind is sharp and painful, like *pi-p'o* (a type of pungent plant).
Regarding the wind called *Viśva-vāyu* among the external winds,
it means the "wind of various skillful adornments."
As it is said, the deity Viśvakarman and others are called "Skillful Deities.
Regarding the Vairambha wind,
this is translated as "whirlwind."
This refers to the violent whirlwind on Mount Sumeru.
As for the "palm of a tala," there is a tree of this kind in the western region.
The leaves resemble those of the palmyra palm;
if one cuts off the leaf tip and retains only the blade, it can still serve as a fan for cooling.
This is explained within the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*.
The initial section refers to the six consciousnesses;
the subsequent mention of "mind, thought,
and consciousness" (citta-manovijñāna) encompasses all eight contaminated consciousnesses.
Question: Just as a noble one (ārya) accomplishes untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) and so forth, may one also designate that which is untainted as a "noble one"?
Answer: One may only generally designate a noble one with respect to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*).
However, it cannot be said that untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) and so forth are established among the six elements (*ṣaddhātu*),
because the six elements are the root of birth.
As for "one who is free from the perception of unity":
One calculates that these elements constitute a self, actually conceiving of the various realms as a body and calculating them to be a unified self;
now, one abandons this notion.
This is what the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to when it says, "The Tathāgata speaks of the notion of a unified whole," and so forth.
In the fifth [section], the contemplation of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
there is first the question and then the explanation.
The conclusion of this meaning follows.
Its explanation consists of two parts.
First is the brief presentation.
The detailed explanation follows later.
Within the preceding section, first the mindfulness is explained,
and subsequently the object of focus is elucidated.
*Āna* means "bringing in" (*cīlai*),
which refers to inhalation.
*Apāna* means "taking away" (*qù*).
This refers to the exhalation. Tāi says:
"In the Tang language, it is called 'holding the breath coming' and 'holding the breath going.'"
In the subsequent detailed explanation,
first the nature of the object of focus— the breath— is explained;
subsequently, the mindfulness that performs the cultivation is analyzed.
The preceding section contains seven sentences:
first, distinguishing that the essence of inhalation and exhalation each has two distinct types;
second, explaining their causes and conditions.
Third, distinguishing the basis of the breath;
fourth, clarifying the practice of the breath;
fifth, clarifying the stage upon which it relies.
Sixth, the explanation of alternative names;
seventh, clarifying that there are two faults in a person who practices the meditation on breath.
Regarding "the inhalation," etc.:
Master Jing’s commentary explains:
when the inhalation enters, it pervades the interior of the body down to the navel region.
As for "the intermediate inhalation":
When the in-breath has ceased and the out-breath has not yet arisen,
there is for a brief interval a subtle wind resembling breath;
this clarifies that mindfulness of the short duration of the in-breath takes this intermediate in-breath as its object.
Regarding the phrase "exhalation is also like this":
from its initial emergence at the navel up to the mouth and nose,
or when it exits outside the nostrils, this is a long exhalation.
When the out-breath has already ceased and the in-breath has not yet arisen,
there is for a brief moment a wind similar to the out-breath between the navel and the nose;
this explains that when mindfulness of the short out-breath is practiced, it takes this intermediate out-breath as its object.
Master Ki says:
"The intermediate inhalation and exhalation" refers to the interval between the two breaths, when although the breathing has not yet entered or exited.
Among these, there are also subtle movements of the breath called intermediate breaths.
In the past, Master Huiyuan said:
"The exhaled breath arises briefly from the navel and reaches the exterior before it ceases."
The inhalation comes from outside the body and enters the body, whereupon it ceases;
its coarseness or subtlety, and its distance or proximity, are not fixed, varying according to the mind.
Tai Ji (Tàijī) says the same.
That breath, through its singular focus, reaches the navel;
because there is no path for the breath below the navel, it has no further place to exit and thus returns until it emerges from the mouth or the tip of the nose.
Regarding the statement that "there are two causes and conditions for the breath," Jing says:
first, the propelling karma is past karma.
The second [condition] refers to the wind-channels that serve as its support and the pores of the skin which serve as its locus; these are also called the causal conditions (*nidāna*).
Tai says:
"First, it is drawn forth by the karmic winds produced by past karma."
Regarding the two small apertures at the navel, or the upper openings of the nostrils, this explains their basis.
As for the statement, "The body is one and the mind is two; in brief, inhalation and exhalation proceed in dependence upon both body and mind, as appropriate," and so forth:
Jingyun: This refers to the *Vibhāṣā* [Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra], which relies on the body and relies on the mind according to what is appropriate and convenient.
"According to what is appropriate and convenient" means:
Some say that the breaths are few during infancy and childhood, but many during middle age and old age.
Others say:
It is called "conducive to suitability" due to four factors:
first, dependence on the body;
second, the passage of the wind-channels.
Third, the pores open.
Fourth, the coarse mind of the earth-element breath manifests before one.
If this were to depend solely on the body and not on the mind, [it would not be possible].
In the two mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), that breath should be understood as having turned back.
At that time, although there exists a body which is the basis for breath and the channels of the wind are also open with the pores dilated,
only the coarse mind is absent from manifesting.
Therefore, the breath does not turn back.
Master Ji said:
"It may depend on the body and mind, or on karma, or on the apertures."
Therefore, it is said "according to what is appropriate.
That which is appropriate as a basis is all that is relied upon.
If [the breath] were to circulate and so forth by relying solely on the body...
In this context, the intention is that the breath does not function solely by depending on the body;
for instance, when one has entered a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*),
although the body remains in a lower realm, that breath does not function.
Therefore, it is not the case that the breaths can function solely by depending on the body;
nor is it the case that they function solely by depending on the mind.
The intention here is to raise an objection: that the breaths cannot function by depending on the mind alone.
If it were not so, then the breath would still function for one who has entered the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
As for the claim that [the breath] functions solely in dependence upon body and mind,
the intended objection here is that the breath can also function in dependence upon apertures, activities, and so forth.
It is not based solely on body and mind;
for instance, during the four stages within the mother's womb, there is no state of being without breath.
Therefore, the treatise speaks of the *kalala* (closed mass) and subsequent stages.
There are two modes of movement for the breaths:
inhalation moves downward because it enters through the nose or mouth and descends toward the navel;
exhalation moves upward because it rises from the navel and proceeds toward the mouth and nose.
Regarding the second stage:
it refers to taking the pathways of the winds and the pores as its basis.
The coarse are the pathways of the winds; the subtle are the pores.
The basis is called "ground" (*bhūmi*).
The preceding [explanation] relies on the pores as the cause; thus, the inhalation and exhalation of breath are termed the "causal condition" (*nidāna-pratyaya*).
There are two faults [in this view].
If the application of skillful means is too lax, it leads to indolence, torpor, and sleep;
if the application of skillful means is too forceful, the raising of the breath becomes constricted,
which can give rise to physical and mental suffering of imbalance.
From here below is the second [section], the explanation of the ability to cultivate mindfulness.
Within this, first five gates are opened,
followed by an explanation based on those gates.
To summarize this later:
according to the *Piṭaka* and other treatises, there are six [factors], namely:
counting (*gaṇanā*), following (*anugama*), settling (*sthāpanā*), observing (*upalakṣaṇā*), transforming (*vivartana*), and purifying (*pariśuddhi*).
Now, this first gateway corresponds to that enumeration;
the other gateways are different.
This explains the first gateway.
First, the four lines are presented;
subsequently, they are explained.
Within this, there are four parts.
First, the explanation of the four lines;
second, the analysis of superior progression and calculation;
third, the analysis of the distinction between the dull and the sharp.
The fourth section is the general summary and conclusion.
Regarding the first point, it says: "Counting one as one.
Jing (Jing) comments:
Because one initially takes the inhalation as the object and does not observe the exhalation, it is said that "the mindfulness abides in the exhalation.
T'ai says:
"This merely takes the inhalation as the object."
However, since mindfulness is established by way of its object,
this is called "mindfulness abiding in inhalation and exhalation.
As for counting the two as one:
The inhalation and exhalation together are counted as one, continuing up to ten.
Regarding "counting in ascending order" (anuloma-gaṇanā):
this refers to the aforementioned two counts from one to ten, which is called "ascending."
Regarding the calculation of retrogression:
for instance, taking one as the starting point within the sequence of numbers, one proceeds from ten down to one—specifically, entering ten and exiting nine;
entering eight and exiting seven; entering six and exiting five; entering four and exiting three; entering two and exiting one.
If one counts by taking two as a single unit,
the first inhalation and exhalation constitute the tenth,
and the subsequent inhalation and exhalation constitute the ninth.
Next, inhalation and exhalation constitute the eighth;
next, inhalation and exhalation constitute the seventh, continuing down to the first.
Question:
If one simply performs the counting in forward order, why resort to counting in reverse?
The explanation says:

it is fundamentally for the purpose of restraining and maintaining [the mind] against excessive discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) that one practices the meditation of counting.
Now, one employs various methods of counting the breaths—
whether as one or many, whether in the forward or reverse order—
to subdue discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), preventing them from arising.
Therefore, he formed this contemplation. Tai said:
"Counting in ascending order up to ten, one does not count eleven, nor does one count nine."
Next, one speaks of eight down to two;
next, one speaks of one.
Therefore, it is called counting in reverse order.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* does not contain this [passage].
Question: Since this mindfulness takes only the present object as its focus, how can it count backward from the tenth through the ninth, eighth, seventh, and so on, into the past?
The Tripitaka Master said:
"One should merely perform a conceptual visualization of the numbers from ten down to nine, and so on, until reaching one."
One does not take the past entities, such as nine or eight, as the basis for counting in reverse.
Second, regarding the explanation of the calculation of progressive advancement:
this refers to the method of counting by taking each single unit as one.
At present, one may either count one inhalation and exhalation together as a single count up to ten,
or count one inhalation and two exhalations, followed by a third inhalation, as a single count up to ten.
Increasing gradually in this manner until fifty inhalations and fifty exhalations are combined;
totaling one hundred breaths constitutes one count, and this is repeated up to ten counts.
If one practices counting by combining two into one,
the first cycle consists of two inhalations and two exhalations, making four breaths counted as one; this proceeds up to ten, and so on,
increasing until there are one hundred inhalations and one hundred exhalations, totaling two hundred breaths.
Combining them into a single count up to ten—
thus the practitioner who diligently cultivates mindfulness of counting breaths takes every ten as one hundred, and so on, until reaching ten such units.
For what reason does one count from one up to ten?
It is because by taking ten as a single unit for calculation,
the mind remains undistracted throughout that interval.
Having completed this naming, one has practiced it thoroughly.
Tai [Zhi] says:
"First, one counts by hundreds as one unit up to the tenth."
This refers to ten, hundred, and thousand.
Furthermore, because ten tens constitute one hundred, it is said that "counting by tens makes one.
Counting gradually in this manner until ten are reached constitutes ten thousand.
Because ten times ten makes one hundred, it is called "ten-tens.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "those who diligently practice the mindfulness of counting breaths," this refers to those who,
while counting from one before reaching ten, experience confusion or errors in the interim.
One should abandon counting [the breaths] that have been missed and begin again from one; this is when,
through extreme familiarity with the practice of counting, [one attains stability].
Furthermore, when there is previously the occurrence of an apprehending subject regarding the inhalation,
one sometimes knows it to exist;
once the inhalation has ceased, there is the occurrence of an apprehending subject regarding the state of emptiness of that breath.
At times one knows it is absent;
subsequently, regarding the exhalation and below,
one knows whether that exhalation is present or absent.
"Thus, through successive continuity and flow, one causes the mind to abide.
This refers to the many contemplative practices explained above that proceed in succession until the mind is made to abide.
Regarding the inhalations and exhalations, one should correctly follow them and thoroughly comprehend them.
Whether they are singular or plural, whether in forward or reverse order, one should correctly follow them without any confusion.
If there is any confusion, one should examine and thoroughly understand it;
that is, one who clearly discerns the distinctions between the phases of inhalation and exhalation, as well as their movement forward and backward during the two intervals.
When the inhalation and exhalation arise, it is called "proceeding" (*pravṛtti*).
When they have already ceased in the interim and have not yet arisen again, it is called "returning" (*nivṛtti*).
To clearly discern such distinctions in the stages of proceeding and returning in this manner is called the cultivation of counting (*gaṇanā-bhāvanā*).
Third, regarding the distinction between those of dull and sharp faculties:
for those of dull faculties,
one teaches counting so that the mind may become settled.
If one employs a method other than counting, one will be entangled and disturbed by torpor and other such hindrances.
However, for those of sharp faculties,
even when taught the method of counting, they are able to comprehend it swiftly and without interruption, and thus do not take pleasure in that practice.
Regarding the fourth section, which summarizes and concludes the preceding points,
according to Jing’s commentary,
it sequentially restates what has gone before.
Because numerous applications of effort serve as causes and conditions, one attains physical and mental pliancy and realizes one-pointedness of mind.
Thus, it is known that the many aforementioned contemplations are all causes for the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and innate [wisdom].
This cultivation results in the attainment of what is called "one-pointedness" (*ekāgratā*),
which is the name for the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
As for the statement "if it functions in this place," this refers back to and concludes the meaning of the four types of counting, beginning with "one as one," and so forth.
"If even up to the point of turning" refers to the superior progression of the aforementioned counting.
"If according to how it turns" [refers to the same].
If there is confusion regarding the preceding bonds, one should return to the beginning and start again.
As for when one proceeds further:
it is when, through the extreme mastery of counting, one knows whether [the breath] exists or does not exist, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "all of this by means of abiding in mindfulness," etc.,
it concludes the preceding discussion on how [the mind] flows in a continuous succession through such successive stages, up until the point where the mind is made to abide, and so forth.
Tai said:
"The names of the various apertures are applied according to their locations;
from their entry into the body down to the navel wheel (nābhi-cakra), they are likewise applied."
Just as the inhalation and exhalation are named according to how they proceed,
so too the duration of the continuity of the inhalation and exhalation— whether long or short— is named according to the time at which it proceeds.
Beiyun said:
If the inhalation begins at the nostrils and ends at the navel wheel,
and the exhalation begins at the site of the navel and reaches the nostrils,
this is called "turning at that place."
The inhalation proceeds gradually from the nose to the navel;
the exhalation proceeds gradually from the navel to the nose.
This is called "if it even turns."
That is to say, when the inhalation and exhalation shift through the nostrils, they follow the path traversed by your two breaths;
thus, their movement is named according to that which they follow.
However, during the meditative attainment of the mindless state (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the inhalation and exhalation cannot proceed.
This [consciousness] transforms during other states;
my [consciousness] transforms while following its course.
This is called "transforming at such-and-such a time."
Jizang further states:
"If it is that which is transformed," this refers back to the aforementioned various apertures.
This refers to the coarse pores, the subtle pores, and so forth;
it is at these locations that the breath turns.
"If it turns even to this extent" means...
That is to say, one brings [the breath] down from the apertures of the body to the navel;
then, as it enters the body, it circulates down to the navel.
If it circulates in this manner:
The preceding [section] on the inhalation and exhalation treats them as a single unit, and so forth;
the remaining periods of breathing proceed according to their respective direct and reverse orders. As for when they proceed:
That is to say, when a practitioner takes one as a unit, or even ten tens as a unit,
and the duration of time— whether long or short— is continuous and so forth, it is termed "time" as it revolves.
At that very time, the counting of the breaths should be shifted.
It is not mentioned again because it has already been accomplished.
This concludes the second [section], the realization of the cultivation of the aggregates.
First, there is a general explanation of the process of realization and entry.
Regarding the statement, "By contemplating the two entities— the grasped object and the grasping subject—

one realizes the aggregates (*skandha*)," this means that by contemplating the nature of the inhaled and exhaled breath as the grasped object and the body upon which it depends, one realizes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Contemplating that the four aggregates occurring simultaneously with the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation—which act as the apprehender—are themselves the entry into the remaining four aggregates.
How does one enter them? Hereafter, the entry is explained in detail.
Tai said:
"For example, when visual consciousness takes blue as its object, this is called direct perception (*pramāṇa*).
At that same time, there is a conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), yet it serves no purpose."
The arising of a seeking mind that "this blue is not yellow" is still a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
because it takes a conventional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*) as its object.
This is called inference (*anumāna*).
If one says that the essence of this atom is blue,
then because its essence is blue, it is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because it does not extend to all that is non-blue,
it is a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If one says, "This is not non-blue," [it is still a specific characteristic].
Apart from the exclusion of blue, there is no separate "non-non-blue.
Therefore, this is a nominal dharma (prajñapti-dharma) and is the object of inference (anumāna).
The meaning of "non-non-blue" pervades all instances of blue.
Therefore, it is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, this blue has "blue-ness" as its essence,
and that essence does not pervade [all instances of blue].
Therefore, it is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
it is not the case that there is no "non-blue" or "non-non-existence," nor does its essence pervade all things.
Therefore, this is a universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
To comprehend this universal characteristic through the mental application of equanimity (*upekṣā-manasikāra*) constitutes the realization of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Simultaneous with this perception, there necessarily exist consciousness (*vijñāna*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
However, because [the faculties] are subtle and inferior, they are not mentioned.
Regarding the third [section], the realization of dependent origination,
there is first a general exposition followed by a specific one.
Within the middle [section], first one seeks the substance of the inhalation and exhalation, which depends upon the body and mind as its conditions;
next, one seeks the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which depends upon the body and mind as its conditions.
These three constitute the substance of birth, aging, and death within the intermediate period.
At the same time, the strong and the weak distinguish between that which produces and that which is produced;
furthermore, one seeks the present life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
which arises from the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of the prior limit.
Furthermore, one investigates that these formations arise from ignorance;
among the ten causes pertaining to the prior limit, the first two— ignorance and formations— are briefly cited.
The preceding section has concluded the reverse-order sequence, which proceeded from the effect back to the cause.
From here on follows the direct order:
having understood in this way that ignorance is the condition for the prior formations, and so forth, up to the point where the body and mind are the conditions for those [formations] to cease.
Thus far, one has entered into the understanding of dependent origination from the perspective of its arising;
furthermore, one understands that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so forth.
Next, one enters into the understanding of dependent origination from the perspective of its cessation.
Fourth, regarding the entry into the Noble Truths:
first, one enters the Truth of Suffering through four principles,
namely, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Knowing that this suffering arises from craving, one penetrates the truth of origination;
furthermore, correctly penetrating that craving for birth gives rise to suffering,
one penetrates the truths of cessation and the path by means of its permanent and complete abandonment without remainder.
The fifty-sixth section, "Supreme Practices," is divided into three parts:
first, restating the preceding summary;
second, the explanation.
This concludes the subsequent section.
First, in order to sever the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), one further practices the sixteen superior modes of activity (*viśeṣa-caryā*).
What is the meaning of the term "superior modes of activity"?
In the past, Master Huiyuan stated that it is called "superior practice" (śikṣā) because of eight causes and conditions.
Master Bei said:
This nature of wisdom is called "superior practice" because it is not shared with non-Buddhists.
To explain now:
it is called "superior practice" because it excels the preceding path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In this commentary, first the enumeration is presented and subsequently explained.
Regarding the enumeration, following the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, seventeen recollections (*saptadaśa-smṛtyupasthāna*) are cited from the sūtras:
one general and sixteen specific.
This treatise is likewise.
Ki says: "In this context, the first is the application of mindfulness through general observation."
Whether long or short, sixteen [factors] are separately enumerated below;
the explanation for these is provided in the middle section of the inquiry.
These sixteen are based upon the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Since ancient times, these have been paired as four sets of four:
first, observing the long breath;
second, observing the short breath.
Third, observing the breath pervading the entire body;
fourth, observing the cessation of bodily formations.
These four constitute the observation of the body.
5. Contemplating joy in the inhalation and exhalation;
6. Contemplating pleasure in the inhalation and exhalation;
7. Contemplating mental formations in the inhalation and exhalation.
Eighth, observing the cessation of mental formations through inhalation and exhalation;
these four observations pertain to feeling.
Ninth, observing the mind through inhalation and exhalation.
10. Contemplating the cessation of the joyful mind.
11. Contemplating the cessation of the restrained and sustained mind.
12. Contemplating the cessation of the liberated mind.
These are the four contemplations of the mind:
the thirteenth is the contemplation of the cessation of impermanence;
the fourteenth is the contemplation of the cessation of severance.
The fifteenth is the contemplation of the cessation of desire;
the sixteenth is the contemplation of the cessation of breath.
These are the four methods of contemplation.
In the explanation of the middle [section], the limits of cultivation are first clarified:
that is, one who has studied and seen the tracks, having already attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment— such as the four foundations of mindfulness—
proceeds with cultivation by applying attention to the object of breath.
In order to sever the remaining fetters, one reflects:
"I shall now train myself in mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation.
This is the second distinct explanation of the sixteen [aspects].
Regarding the four aspects of the body,
the Tripiṭaka Master says:

Regarding the awareness of the breath pervading the entire body:
when first observing the breath, it is focused solely at the tip of the nose.
Later, when the contemplation is accomplished, one is able to know that those breaths enter and exit pervading the entire body;
therefore, it receives the name "awareness.
As for the cessation of bodily formations:
Bodily activity refers to inhalation and exhalation;
causing these breaths to cease is called the cessation of bodily activity.
Regarding "among the four feelings," and furthermore,
"one who thus discerns joy, one who discerns pleasure, and so forth"—
this explains the mental formations therein.
There may be false thoughts arising such as "I" and "mine," or the conceit "I shall possess formlessness, etc.
Master Ji explains:
these views are called "momentary false thoughts" (*kṣaṇika-vikalpa*) because they arise for a brief duration.
This is not a view among the sixty-two views.
If one were to rely on these sixty-two views,
I would possess this view of eternalism.

then those who have previously seen the truths perform these sixteen superior practices (*viśeṣa-caryā*).
How can views such as the perception of permanence arise?

The preceding discussion on those who have seen the truth (dṛṣṭasatya) is based on persons who have realized the truth;

the arising of views such as eternalism serves as proof.

Having attained that concentration— the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first *dhyāna*—

Regarding the one who, within the five stages of the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) of the desire realm, effects abandonment, detachment, and cessation of the elements:
according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 72, it says:
The three realms of abandonment and so forth are distinguished by taking the previously mentioned unconditioned state, termed "liberation," as their intrinsic nature.
However, while these three realms differ in terms of conventional designation (*prajñapti*),
they are without distinction when considered in terms of actual reality (*dravya*).
What is meant by "difference based on conventional designation"?
It refers to designating the abandonment of the fetter of attachment as the "element of abandonment" (prahāṇadhātu),
and the severance of the remaining eight fetters as the "element of cessation" (nirodhadhātu).
The cessation of all entities bound by the fetters of greed and other defilements is called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
For what reason are the three elements thus differentiated?
It is because contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are, in brief, of three kinds.
First, those that can bind but cannot defile;
second, those that both bind and defile;
third, those dharmas that neither [bind nor defile] but accord with binding and defiling.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized through the abandonment of these three factors is respectively termed the "abandonment" and so forth of the three realms.
Now, this Mahāyāna is not the same as that.
Question: At what stage do these sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) first come to be cultivated?
Master Yuan said:
"Speaking in general terms,
from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), all practice this contemplation."
If explained according to their distinct characteristics:
the first four begin with the contemplation during the five stages of cessation of the mind (*pañca-vinodana-citta*),

Third, below this, is the explanation of the skillful objects of focus (*kauśalyālambana*).

Second, the sequential explanation.

If one follows the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Vibhāṣā*), the sixth fascicle states that there are four wholesome dharmas:

If one follows this fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it speaks of five types of skillfulness (*kauśalya*).
The *Fifty-seven [Treatises]* speaks of six types of expertise (*kauśalya*);

The *Exposition of the Mahāyāna*, chapter fourteen, speaks of seven types of expertise.
Furthermore, regarding skillfulness in thorough discernment,

Second, the elements;

six: the faculties;

The eight truths,
the nine vehicles,

The seventeenth fascicle of the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* explains the ten skillful means (*kauśalya*).
First, the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha-dharma*);
second, the elements (*dhātu*).
The three bases,
the four truths,
and the five analytical knowledges.
Sixth is the reliances (*pratisaraṇa*), namely the four reliances such as relying on the meaning rather than the letter.
Seventh is the provisions (*sambhāra*).
Eighth is the factors of the path (*mārgadharma*), namely the thirty-seven [auxiliaries] (*saptatriṃśatprakāra*).
Ninth, dependent origination;
tenth, the universal inclusion of all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned.
This concludes the explanation within the skill in the aggregates.
What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)? Regarding the so-called "with signs" (*sanimitta*) and "without signs" (*animitta*):
perception that takes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its object is called "with signs";
perception that takes ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its object is called "without signs."

Furthermore, taking as an object a phenomenon that possesses substantial reality—namely, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—is called "having signs" (*sanimitta*).
Taking as an object a phenomenon lacking substantial reality—the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Taking the desire realm as an object is called "small signs."
That which takes the form realm as its object is called "vast.
That which takes the sphere of infinite space or the sphere of infinite consciousness as its object is called "immeasurable.
The absence of all that exists is the sphere of nothingness.
The aggregate of consciousness refers to the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and awareness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
The first states:
That is to say, the substance of the six consciousnesses is called "mind" (*citta*) because it has the sense of accumulating and arising;
it is called "intellect" (*manas*) because it has the sense of deliberating and reflecting; and it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it has the sense of discerning and distinguishing.
One explanation states:
the ālayavijñāna is called "mind" (citta),
while the manas is termed "intellect" (manas).
The six consciousnesses are called "consciousness.
Regarding the statement that the preceding aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as this aggregate of consciousness, all possess the past and so forth:
it should be understood that the substance of these four aggregates—feeling and the others—pervades the three periods of time.
If they take external objects as their object, they are called "external" according to those objects;
if they take the internal body as their object, they are called "internal" according to those objects.
The four aggregates associated with the five consciousnesses are termed "coarse."
The four aggregates associated with mental consciousness are called "subtle.
These four aggregates, when characterized by the nature of goodness, are called "excellent";
those of the other two natures are called "evil."
The past and the future are called "distant.
Because the future has not yet arisen and the past has already ceased, they do not abide in the present body; therefore, they are called distant.
The present is called "near."
Regarding skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*):

if one further regards those eighteen kinds of phenomena as being "skill in the elements," it is because the essential nature of the eighteen elements is correctly apprehended as the seeds capable of producing [phenomena], and these are taken to be the elements.
However, as for the statement in the text that the eighteen dharmas— the eye, visible objects, visual consciousness, and so forth— are also called "elements" (dhātu),
this is designated as an "element" by way of association rather than being the actual essence of an element.
Therefore, it further states that these eighteen kinds of dharmas arise and appear from their respective elements, respective seeds, and respective lineages.
Therefore, one should know that the eighteen kinds of dharmas are not the actual substance of the *dhātu*.
The three terms—*dhātu*, seed (*bīja*), and lineage (*gotra*)—differ in name but are identical in substance;
they all share the seed as the substance of the eighteen *dhātus*.
Now, one who seeks to fully understand that the seeds of the eighteen kinds of phenomena are each distinct is said to be skilled in the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, among the four conditions, such a person attains skill in them as being equivalent to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding skill in the bases (*āyatana-kuśala*):
it means understanding that the twelve bases function as three conditions to produce the six consciousnesses;
the simultaneous dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the sixth consciousness is precisely the *manas*.
Therefore, the treatise states: "This attention (*manasikāra*) acts as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It may also be that the attention associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) simultaneously acts as the predominant condition.
According to this principle, the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharma-āyatana*) together act as conditions to produce the mental consciousness.
This means that the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are not explained as before;
rather, within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is simply stated that "only dharmas moisten dharmas."
There are two kinds of moisture:
first, that which moistens, which is craving;
second, that which is moistened, which consists of existence (*bhava*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth.
Equal moisture also has two aspects.
That which is moistened is the same as before;
that which moistens is grasping (*upādāna*), which is also called "nourishing moisture" because it is desirable.
The remaining afflictions that assist and moisten birth are called "equal moistening.
The ten causes are termed "projectors," and the two fruits are termed "projected."
Therefore, below, birth, aging, and death are set forth as being among the *saṃskāras*.
Alternatively, all twelve links of dependent origination may be termed *saṃskāras*.
That which directly produces [an effect] is called the "cause."
"Assisting in discernment is called 'condition' (pratyaya).

Furthermore, it should be understood that skill in what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya) is a specific differentiation of skill in dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya)," etc.
This is because the fifth [topic], skill in what is possible and impossible, emerges from the perspective of dependent origination.
What is the distinction?
Herein, the initial thought generally clarifies that ignorance conditions wholesome and unwholesome formations to obtain the fruits of future birth, aging, and death;
it does not clarify the locus by means of an unequal cause.
That which differs from this is called "improper" (*asthāna*).
Later, when it is specifically explained that wholesome dharmas produce desirable fruits while unwholesome ones produce undesirable fruits and so forth, this is called "proper" (*sthāna*);
that which differs from this is called "improper."
The five [categories] are subsumed within the two [types of skill].
Regarding how skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) manifests as skill in specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*):
it was explained above that within skill in the aggregates there are three meanings.
First, the nature of various distinctions;
second, the nature of being manifold rather than one;
third, that apart from these phenomena, nothing further can be apprehended or conceptually differentiated.
Based on the first two meanings, skillfulness is distinguished as being its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
As for how skillfulness in the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is revealed by the remaining skillfulnesses:
it is because there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*) that are alike in their causal conditions, and thus one attains skillfulness therein.
One attains skillfulness regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*) by means of the three conditions;
one attains skillfulness regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by means of their being impermanent and so forth.

Within the categories of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), the general explanation of the equality of cause and effect across the three time periods of dependent origination is termed "the possible" (*sthāna*).
The term "impossible" (*asthāna*) refers to an unequal cause and effect;
therefore, the other four types of skillfulness are collectively termed "common characteristics.
In the fourth [section], regarding the object of focus for purifying the afflictions:
First, it clarifies that on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), one contemplates the lower realms as coarse (*audārika*) and the upper realms as tranquil (*śānta*);
having thus suppressed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one returns to cultivate them.
Second, it clarifies that on the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), which takes the four noble truths as its object, one abandons all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the various afflictions.
Although the methods of subduing and severing differ, both are termed "paths for purifying afflictions.

Regarding the statement that the nature of the aggregates is coarse—that is, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) in the desire realm consists of many categories that should be known and severed—it should be understood as follows.
For example, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are the male and female faculties, as well as forms such as odor and flavor;
these are absent in the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, among the four aggregates (*skandha*), the desire realm possesses three feelings (*vedanā*) associated with the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
The first dhyāna is not like this;
since perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) can be understood according to their respective meanings, they are all relatively coarse.
In this same manner, one should consider each successive stage in relation to the higher stages.
In all lower stages, there is much suffering and affliction and life is diminished;
in the higher stages, there is little suffering and life is increased—
this is the characteristic of the coarse and the tranquil.
Next, the objects of focus for purifying afflictions through the supramundane path are explained;
these are the knowledges of the Four Noble Truths.
Within this, first the general enumeration is presented.
Next is the explanation,
followed by the conclusion.
