First, the essence of the truths is presented;
second, the meaning of the truths is explained;
third, the meaning of the noble truths is explained.
The fourth section further explains the distinctions among categories of meaning, such as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), following the arising of suffering.
Regarding the first part, there is first the teaching and then the illustration.
Within the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), it says: "If it is craving..."
This sentence is a general statement.
If one possesses craving for future existence,
one seeks craving for the internal body.
The latter two types of craving are craving for external objects.
Regarding objects already obtained, it is called craving accompanied by delight and lust;
regarding objects not yet obtained, it is the arising of "this-and-that" craving for pleasure and delight.
Regarding "one who is able to attain and able to realize":
one accumulates the path that attains [cessation] and realizes the cessation of suffering.
Question: According to the Abhidharma, among the eight types of suffering—
The first seven are the objects of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);
the last one is the object of supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*).
Why, then, does this treatise designate all eight types of suffering as the objects of supramundane knowledge?
Answer: Worldly knowledge is of two kinds:
first, the knowledge of the six practices;
second, the knowledge of the noble practices.
In the *Abhidharma*, because it concerns the wisdom of noble practice (*ārya-caryā*), it takes the preceding seven [stages] as suffering;
this treatise, however, based on the wisdom of the six modes of conduct (*ṣad-ākāra-jñāna*), takes them as coarse and calm.
Thus, there is no contradiction in meaning.
Furthermore, that treatise establishes the Truth of Suffering based on its predominant aspects;
therefore, it does not include the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) or the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
It establishes the [other] three truths based on their totality.
Therefore, it is said that the cessation of all afflictions and karma, along with their antidotes, are designated as the three truths.
This treatise establishes the truth of suffering based on the totality [of these factors],
while establishing the other three truths based on their predominant aspects.
Question: Greed (*lobha*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) differ in name but are identical in essence.
Why, then, is it said that "craving accompanied by joy and greed"?
Answer: According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
By this, it is definitively known that the designation "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is established based on all afflictions in general;
otherwise, it would not be appropriate to call it "concomitant with greed" (*lobha-sahagata*).
Now, [the author] explains:
In this text, joy is associated with craving, and craving itself is termed "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*);
it cannot be said that craving is associated with thirst.
This is as explained in the section on the meaning of the Truths.
Regarding the statement that "the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) is called 'truth' because its meaning as suffering, up to its being non-perverted, is [so designated]":
this explains "truth" (satya) by way of the sense of being non-perverted;
it refers to the teaching of the *Vipula-vinaya* (or *Upadeśa*) that actual suffering cannot be made into happiness, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not deceptive and so forth,
this corresponds to what is said in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*:
"Moreover, because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not false, and because one perceives them and thereby attains non-erroneous cognition, they are called truths (*satya*)."
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are briefly five meanings:
first, reality; second, truth; third, suchness; fourth, non-perversion; and fifth, non-falsity.
In this present text, there are likewise five meanings.
First, it is as it is; second, it is real; third, it is non-erroneous; fourth, it is not false; fifth, by seeing it, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the explanation of the distinctions among the categories of meaning, the initial explanation of the Truth of Suffering is divided into two parts.
First, the meaning of the eight sufferings has been briefly explained so that it may be understood.
Next, the three sufferings are elucidated;
herein there are three parts.
"Subsuming one into eight makes three;
that is to say, through various perspectives such as arising and so forth, it is only the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the others that are revealed.
Jing says:
Because they are categorized according to different perspectives, the first seven types of suffering manifest only as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*),
since causes such as birth give rise predominantly to painful sensations.
Within the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha-duḥkha*), all three types of suffering are fully present.
Why is this? Just as the five aggregates of clinging fully encompass the three types of sensation,
they serve as the vessel for the aforementioned suffering of suffering.
This also entails the two types of suffering associated with change and formations.
If one were to discuss them by subsuming them through a general approach according to their meaning,
each of the eight sufferings possesses all three types of suffering.
Master Ji said:
"To regard the seven types of suffering as the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) is spoken of according to the actual reality."
As for other passages that state only the first five [aggregates] constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*),
this is because they speak of the suffering of suffering in terms of its predominant aspect.
The two questions and answers serve to distinguish these names.

Question: For what reason are the other two types of suffering described using the terms "disintegration" (*bhaṅga*) and "change" (*anyathātva*), while the first is described using the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*) itself?
Answer: There are four reasons for this.
First, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) are known only by the noble ones (*ārya*);
however, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is perceived even by the ignorant.
Therefore, it is spoken of using its own specific name.
Second, the suffering of suffering is extremely loathsome.
Third, as soon as the suffering of suffering is mentioned, it is easily understood.
Fourth, when sentient beings who are capable of being converted hear this teaching, they enter into the Truths with ease.
Third, the establishment of the three types of suffering:
the preceding seven sufferings manifest the suffering of sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*) and the four aggregates that serve as its basis;
these five aggregates, taken collectively, are termed the "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
It is established within the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
That is to say, all states of existence (*bhava*) are the objects to be countered by the remaining six types of suffering, excluding birth.

Furthermore, there is the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*), as well as the bases upon which that sensation depends—whether the sense faculties (*indriya*) or their objects (*viṣaya*)—and the afflictions (*kleśa*) produced by those conditions.
Furthermore, there are causes such as prior health that give rise to pleasant feelings, as well as the afflictions produced by those pleasant feelings;
these, taken together, are collectively described as the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
This is based on the supreme authoritative teaching (*āptāgama*), which is the foremost authoritative teaching.
The old [translation] says "sacred teaching" (shèngjiào),
but this term does not exist in the Sanskrit original;
it simply says "ultimate teaching" (zhìjiào).
Because it is the teaching of the ultimate truth,
and while the ultimate teachings are numerous— some of which are explicit and others implicit—
it is called "the foremost" here because it cites the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "the suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), a designation not found in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Because the meaning of "suffering" is difficult to discern, it is necessary to cite scriptural authority.
For this reason, based on the principle of the suffering of change, it applies universally throughout the three realms.
Since other sources state only that there is pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*),
the nature of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is established from the third dhyāna downward.
As for the statement, "If the nature of conditioned suffering pervades all five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādānaskandha*)," and so forth:
The impermanence of the aggregates of appropriation is called *saṃskāra*.
Because whenever there is craving for any of the three feelings, a state of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and lack of pliancy is constantly pursued;
since the essence of those formations (*saṃskāra*) is thus unstable, it is termed the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
To state it briefly:
excluding those phenomena subsumed under the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change, there are those associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

or those phenomena produced by that equanimity-feeling; or the conditions for the arising of that equanimity-feeling; or the aggregates upon which the arising of equanimity-feeling depends and abides, along with their arising and ceasing in association.
All these are the essence of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because these formations are accompanied by the four types of clinging (*upādāna*), the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*), and the heavy residues (*dausthulya*), they cannot attain stability and are thus called the "suffering of formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Furthermore, it is subsequently stated that they do not escape the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and that they proceed without mastery.

If one follows the principle of transformation at dawn, although one abandons the substance of feeling, because the seeds of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) have not been relinquished, it is called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
Even if one manifests the feeling of suffering, one still cannot escape the seeds of the other two types of suffering.

If one relies on the gateway of ultimate truth, the equanimity of the ālayavijñāna is the essence of formative forces (saṃskāra); because it is constantly accompanied by the seeds of the other two types of suffering, it is called the suffering of formative forces (saṃskāraduḥkhatā).
Below, the latter three truths are explained.
Regarding the cessation of the basis (*āśraya-nirodha*),
one interpretation states that it is the cessation of maturation (*vipāka*).
One explanation states:
the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) takes the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its basis;
because this cognitive hindrance is extinguished, it is called the "extinction of the basis."
The explanation of the objects of focus is completed.
From here below is the fourth section, the explanation of the gate of instruction.
Within this, first, the four kinds of instruction are explained.
Later, regarding the explanation of the three types of instruction,
Tái says:
"Because one gives rise to reverence upon seeing the miraculous transformations."
By focusing one's mind and lending an ear to hear the Dharma and contemplate it, one generates reverence.
By means of the wheel of others' minds, one seeks out the specific modes of others' minds, such as greed and so forth.
By means of the wheel of the exhaustion of outflows, [one acts] according to the faculties of the three vehicles.
Just as there are the skillful means of the three vehicles, so too is the true Dharma taught for the sake of awakening to and entering the Noble Truths according to the three vehicles.

Alternatively, it may be understood that the practice of transforming others is subsumed by these three wheels: the three grades of faculties and conduct, and the awakening to and entry into the Truths.
There is nothing it does not accomplish;
therefore, it is called the perfection of the characteristics of inclusion.
This is from the twenty-eighth section of the main treatise, the fifth explanation within the three trainings.
First, there are three correct understandings;
next, the three faculties are established based on the three trainings;
and finally, the three doors of liberation are established based on the training in concentration.
In the preceding section, there are six gates:
first, the differentiation of the essence of the three trainings;
second, the explanation of the reason why there are only three.
Third, distinguishing the sequence of priority;
fourth, distinguishing the reason why the three trainings are designated as "supreme" (adhipati);
fifth, clarifying the extent of their accomplishment.
Sixth, it clarifies that while there are differences in how one enters the noble state and attains the fruits based on these three trainings,

the subsequent text of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* also states that it is by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that one is first able to enter the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.
That is to say, one who knows and sees the Four Noble Truths as they truly are is called a learner in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śaikṣa*).
Master Basit explains:
"This refers exclusively to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) when it is designated as the training in wisdom."
This is not called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
If one follows the previous explanation regarding the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*),
the first instance refers exclusively to the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas when speaking of the training in concentration.
How is this known? The subsequent passage states:

"Thus, it is by relying on dhyāna that one is first able to enter the clear observation of the Noble Truths and the state of rightness beyond birth; it is not the case that one can accomplish this matter while being entirely devoid of all dhyānas."
This is a further explanation.
The first interpretation explains that the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) refers exclusively to the four dhyānas.

The second interpretation, moreover, holds that all formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and all other meditative absorptions (*samādhi* and *samāpatti*) are also called the training in concentration.

That is to say, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and all other remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) are called the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
This [training in concentration] thus encompasses both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Why is it that the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) is exclusively uncontaminated, while the training in concentration encompasses both?
The commentary states:
"That concentration is likewise exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The previous mention of 'furthermore, the formless concentrations' refers to untainted concentrations."
Furthermore, all other meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) are also termed the "training in concentration" (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
This refers specifically to the untainted (*anāsrava*) concentrations of the four dhyānas that can induce the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
There is no contradiction in maintaining that the training in concentration consists solely of untainted [wisdom], as its meaning is identical to that of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, meditative absorption (samādhi) and supernormal powers (abhijñā) are both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava); the same applies to wisdom (prajñā).
This statement is made from the perspective of those that are preeminent as being without outflows.
There is no impediment to employing different meditative requisites or methods.
According to the following passage: "If one possesses ethical discipline and concentration, one does not necessarily possess wisdom;
if one possesses wisdom, one necessarily possesses ethical discipline and concentration."
Therefore, the former interpretation is superior,
as it takes untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as the training (*śikṣā*).

Furthermore, what prevents the training in wisdom from being exclusively untainted, while the trainings in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) may include both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted?
There is no impediment to the unevenness of their breadth.
Within the explanation of the meaning of "predominance" (*adhipati*),
two gates are first opened.
Next, the explanation:
the latter part remains to be further clarified.

There is superior wisdom that induces superior mind, as in the case of the noble disciple up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; there is superior mind that induces wisdom, as previously described.

Since the previous explanation— that one cultivates the concentrated mind for the sake of superior wisdom— did not fully exhaust this meaning, it is now restated here within the section on the accomplishment of understanding.
First, the extent of that accomplishment is distinguished.
Regarding the subsequent exhortation to practice:

"There is superior ethical discipline, but not the other two" means that there is the prātimokṣa vow for one who has not yet attained meditative concentration; this is stated as "not having them" because it refers to the wisdom born of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).

Regarding those who possess ethical discipline and meditative concentration but lack wisdom: this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because they have attained mundane concentration and thus lack the untainted wisdom of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-prajñā*).
Among the different types of entry into the noble state and attainment of the fruits, the first is one who has not yet abandoned desire.

When one is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), if the afflictions have not yet been subdued, or if they have been subdued up to the fifth category of the desire realm's cultivated afflictions, one is said to be "not yet free from desire.
One who is "twice-free from desire" (dvitīya-vītarāga) is as follows:
First, one subdues six grades up to eight grades.
As for those who have already become free from desire,
they have already subdued the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Up to the point where one has suppressed the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness and is said to have "already abandoned desire," it should be understood that herein,
there are those who have not yet completely abandoned any desire whatsoever.
Regarding those who enter the clear realization of the truths and realize the fruit of stream-entry:
this refers, for the time being, to those who have not yet suppressed any of the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
therefore, it is said that they have not yet abandoned desire entirely.
One who has subdued the five grades through the path of reasoning also realizes the first fruit (*srotāpatti*).
One who is "doubly detached from desire" has abandoned six of the nine grades;
this is termed "doubly detached from desire."
Regarding the establishment of the three faculties:
this refers to the sequential arrangement of those ten faculties within three stages.
As for what are called the "ten faculties":
That is to say, the five faculties beginning with faith, the mental faculty, and the faculties of sorrow, joy, pleasure, and equanimity— these ten faculties,

when they exist within the seven stages of preparation (*prayoga*) and during the fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
If, while in the stage of expedient means, one has not yet correctly known the principle of the Truths but is about to know them correctly, it is called "the unknown that should be known.
If, at the time of the fifteenth moment of mind, one has not yet known [the Truths] repeatedly but is about to know them repeatedly, it is called "the unknown that should be known."
From the sixteenth moment of mind onwards, it is termed the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*).
Since one has already seen the truth and there is no further meaning of "not yet known" to be known,
this faculty persists as the faculty of "already known" throughout the stages up until the exhaustion of desire.
However, if one has already abandoned desire, the faculty of sorrow is eliminated, and only the remaining nine faculties constitute the faculty of "one who knows" (ājñendriya).
Within the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), these same nine faculties constitute the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
However, according to the *Viniścaya*, it is said that the Wheel of Dharma was turned with three revolutions and twelve aspects.
These three revolutions refer to the teaching of these three faculties (*indriya*).
That is to say, when the Buddha spoke of the bodhisattva, his initial knowledge of suffering and so forth is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

For the sake of exhausting the remaining outflows (*āsrava*), one should further understand that the [knowledges] regarding the origin of suffering and so forth are called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).

At the time of attaining Buddhahood, the [knowledges] such as "I have already known suffering, I have already abandoned its origin, I have already realized cessation, and I have already cultivated the path" are called the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Regarding the establishment of the three liberations within the training in concentration:
it is said that there are two aspects to the objects of knowledge—
existence and non-existence.
Existence is further divided into two:
the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The wishless (apraṇihita) is established by taking the five aggregates of clinging as its object.
The signless (*animitta*) is established by taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object;
emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is established because [the mind] takes as its objects such things as the self and sentient beings, which are non-existent dharmas.
By this passage, it is explained that the gate of emptiness is established by taking emptiness and the absence of self (*anātman*) as its objects.
Based on the four aspects of the origin of suffering and impermanence, the wishless (*apraṇihita*) is established;
based on the four aspects of cessation, the signless (*animitta*) is established.
The term "wishless" is used to distinguish it from the signless, as the latter is devoid of any aspiration.
"Non-existence of aspiration" excludes wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Just as that which is not existent is known to be non-existent and established as the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*),
the four lower aspects of the path are not the three doors of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).
The other categories are extensively distinguished;
their mutual inclusion is as previously described.
In the sixth section, the explanation of the dharmas conducive to training (*śikṣānulomika-dharma*), it says:
There are two sets of ten dharmas.
Within the first set of ten, one first presents the obstacles that are to be remedied.
Next, the ten contemplations that serve as the remedies are presented in their proper sequence to counteract [the ten objects].
Among the ten objects to be remedied,
two concern the arising of attachment toward the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) subsumed under the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Regarding the formations of the body, one conceives them as permanent and becomes attached to them.
Third, those who are indolent and lazy become indolent because they are attached to pleasure and self-comfort.
Regarding the phrase "the various worldly conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*)": for the sake of one's body and life,
one engages in agriculture,
commerce, and service to the king.
Medical prescriptions and incantations;
the construction of gardens and pavilions;
singing, laughter, and the chanting of poetry, and so forth.
All of these are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
There are eleven types of faults associated with the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) of yoga when contemplating all phenomena (*dharma*).
First is doubt.
Second, due to coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), one is unable to take pleasure in abandoning [defilements] or taking pleasure in cultivation.
Third, due to lethargy and sleep, one is lax and negligent regarding the means for cultivating calm abiding and insight.
Fourth, the obstacle of physical exhaustion and mental affliction to fierce diligence;
fifth, the obstacle of inferior and meager diligence leading to the decline of wholesome qualities;
sixth, the obstacle of delighting in fame and profit.
Seventh, agitation;
eighth, giving rise to fear toward nirvāṇa;
ninth, engaging in improper and forceful speech out of a desire for victory over others, thereby inciting strife and litigation.
Tenth, the mind races and scatters toward various objects.
Eleventh, one forcefully contemplates matters that should not be contemplated.
These are all faults resulting from the darkness of the mind, which fails to clearly understand phenomena through its reflections.
This is then countered below by the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*).
There are four kinds of light:
first, the light of the Dharma (*dharmāloka*).
This refers to the name given because the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) thoroughly understands the teachings.
Second is the "light of meaning," which refers to the name given because the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) definitively discerns the meaning.
The latter two may be understood.
Master Jing’s judgment states:

"Among these eleven [types of ignorance], if one’s mind is darkened or deluded regarding the teachings, it should be remedied by the light of the Dharma through the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*)."
If the mind gives rise to obscurations regarding the meaning elucidated by the teachings, one remedies this with the light of the meaning of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
If that which hinders the engagement in practice acts as an obscuration, one remedies it with the light of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, in this context, one may simply take the light of the Dharma and its meaning as heard and reflected upon to remedy all the faults involved in contemplating phenomena;
one does not take the light of śamatha and vipaśyanā as the remedy.
Since this very śamatha and vipaśyanā constitute the essence of training,
the present section clarifies only those dharmas that accord with training and does not clarify the essence of training itself; therefore,
śamatha and vipaśyanā are excluded.
Therefore, in the passage below, after citing the four types of light, it immediately specifies:
"In this present context, the intended meaning is to include those who can sever the obstacles to the yoga-attention that contemplates all phenomena."
Before one has attained hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*), contemplating various phenomena cannot constitute an obstacle;
however, because one has now attained hearing and reflection, one is able to eliminate and sever them.
Master Basit further said:
In this present context, the intention in taking up "those capable of severing" and so forth is to explain that,
as in the preceding case of light, there are only four types; specifically,
it intends to include both the light of the Dharma and the light of meaning, which are capable of severing those factors that obstruct the yoga of contemplation.
Regarding the phrase "past causes" within the latter ten dharmas—
referring to the perfection of the faculties through prior cultivation—
it means that in previous lives one cultivated the faculties such as faith, which were then perfected, accumulated, and increased.
"Conformity with the teaching" refers to the taught doctrine.
"Unerring sequence" means that when one hears the teaching on the initial stage of practice.

First one cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*), next one attains entry into the state of an Arya, then one gives rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and finally one reaches the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Hearing such an explanation of the sequence of cultivation, the mind can accord with this unerring teaching.
Regarding the cessation of the coarseness (*dausthulya*) of body and mind, there are four successive stages.
In the first two, the coarseness arises from the mental engagement with those forms;
it is then brought to rest by means of that very engagement, becoming easily relinquished.
The third type of *dausthulya* is that which is produced by lethargy and sleep; it is ceased by means of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that apprehends pure and sublime signs through wisdom.
The fourth type of *dausthulya* has the afflictions as its cause; because this causal continuity exists, it is brought to cessation through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This text clearly explains the characteristics of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
It is not merely the residual force of those afflictions (*kleśa*) that is an unpliant nature;
it also refers to the failure to engage in what should be done and the failure to desist from what should not be done.
Regarding those who perform what is wholesome and do not regress from it:
they do not regress from performing what is wholesome, yet they do not perform that which should not be done.
Therefore, it is said that they "do not regress from non-action and are free from overweening pride."
One does not conceive the notion of attainment regarding what has not been attained;
one is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*);
and one conceives the notion of attainment regarding what has actually been attained. Thus it is said.
Having clearly understood the limits [of these stages], one reaches the seventh: the dissolution of yoga.
As for the ultimate dissolution of yoga:
This refers to those who lack the seed of nirvāṇa and are ultimately lost to supramundane concentration and wisdom.
Those who are temporarily lost are those who possess the seed of nirvāṇa but have not yet attained it due to the absence of external conditions.
Regarding "those who have fallen away from what was attained and are ruined," Jing says:
it is like those such as stream-enterers who, having previously suppressed the desires of the desire realm, subsequently attain the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the higher realms.
Regarding "meeting conditions and falling away from abiding in peace and so forth," Tai says:
"Falling away refers to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative concentrations and their associated knowledge and vision that ordinary persons have contacted and realized."
The Master [Sthiramati] merely states:
"It refers precisely to tainted meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the like.
As for "the yoga that is corrupted by the performance of wrong conduct":

Although one may possess the lineage for nirvāṇa, if one practices improperly or acts with hypocrisy, even if one cultivates the three trainings, it is not truly called "yoga" because it does not accord with the principles of the Tripiṭaka. It is a corruption.
This can be seen by examining the text.
Tai says:
"There may be some practitioners whose nature is characterized by a preponderance of afflictions."
One whose awakening-wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) is so sharp and intense that it arises spontaneously,
being by nature acute and possessing innate discernment, immediately loses the yoga;
such is the disciple who turns back.
Master Ji said:
"It is called 'reversal' because it follows that teaching.
This is from the eighth section, the Explanation of Yoga.
Regarding the two aspects of faith,
Jing says: first,
the aspect of compliant faith.
This refers to the arising of faith and compliance in the mind when hearing the teachings on the Truths, the Jewels, and so forth.
Regarding the second characteristic, purity:
indeed, a lack of faith is called impurity.
Now, it is taught that faith and compliance are termed the "aspects of pure conduct.
According to the Abhidharma-śāstra,
patience (kṣānti) is the aspect of practice, while faith is the aspect of compliant practice.
The characteristic of pure conduct is the name "pure conduct.
Regarding the two bases:
first is the basis of observing the principles of all phenomena.
For instance, when one hears the exposition of the principles of the Four Noble Truths,
one observes therein that the causes and effects of defilement and purity truly exist and are not false;
based upon this, one gives rise to faith.
Therefore, it is called the "basis.
Second, regarding the basis of the supernatural power of the individual characterized by faith and understanding:
it refers to seeing manifest miraculous transformations.
Therefore, faith arises;
it is also called the basis.
Among the four [desires], it is desire.
Regarding "those who desire to conform to yoga," this refers to those who generate longing and so forth while practicing the path through uninterrupted application and earnest application;
these two types of application are the conforming practices.
All practices are themselves yoga.
Now, for the sake of seeking the two types of application that accord with yoga, a mind of longing arises;
this longing is desire (*chanda*).
Regarding the four skillful means,
Master Jing’s commentary states:
first, to protect the śīla (precepts) by properly guarding one's mindfulness.
Second, non-negligence;
third, single-mindedly and correctly cultivating śamatha within;
fourth, the superior wisdom of dharma-vipaśyanā.
Taigi said the same:
first, śīla;
second, mindfulness.
Third is non-negligence;
fourth is concentration and wisdom.
Master Tai also provides this interpretation.
There may be other skillful means different from these that one might bring up when questioning the Dharma Master.
The Dharma Master says:
"The meanings of skillful means and yoga are manifold."
To fixate upon any single one [of these] would contradict reason.
If we rely on the inclusion of the eight *prahāṇasaṃskāras* within the twenty-nine [factors] below, it is stated that their essence consists of the five factors of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
The ninth section, "Explanation of Mental Application" (*manasikāra*), contains three parts:
first, the analysis of two types of fourfold mental applications;
second, the clarification of the characteristics of what is contemplated through mental application.
Next, it clarifies how mental attention (manasikāra) arises with respect to its object through nine types of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
Regarding "mental attention that functions with strenuous effort":
this refers to a beginner who has not yet attained a concentrated mind fixed on the form realm (rūpadhātu).
However, within the desire realm, through the power of hearing and reflection, one exerts the mind in distraction and settles it inwardly,
abiding in equipoise. Or, one correctly discerns all phenomena,
until one attains the mental attention of the stage of meditative concentration that has been cultivated.
Regarding those who apply themselves with diligence during hearing and reflection, yet practice in an intermittent manner:
this refers to having already attained the mental attention cultivated within the *anāgamya* concentration through the preparatory stages of hearing and reflection.
From this point onward, one may gradually progress through both mundane and supramundane paths,
attaining the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that has been cultivated; therein,
the "discernment of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) comes first.
It is still interspersed with the conceptual wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) of the desire realm and the emergence and entry of formal signs (*nimitta*);
because it cannot proceed exclusively as a purely concentrated mind,
it is called "interrupted" (*sāntara*).
The Master Tai and others say:
*manasikāra* (attention) is called "recollection" (*smṛti*).
However, it is designated as "concentration" (*samādhi*) when associated with concentration, and thus concentration itself is termed "attention."

"Uninterrupted operation" means that from the initial attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*), one enters into the subsequent five types of attention;
thus, they can proceed in succession without being interrupted by the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).
The culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga-niṣṭha*) refers to the three final uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) following the abandonment of desire.
That which operates without effort (*anābhoga-vāhana*) refers to the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*).
This is the fruit of the ninth liberation of one who has abandoned desire.

Having completed the abandonment of desire, there is no further effort required regarding the afflictions of the desire realm; furthermore, there remain four other types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

The initial attention that accords with reality (*anulomamanasikāra*) is still part of the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedimanaskāra*) and a portion of the attention of joyful engagement (*ratisaṃgrāhakamanaskāra*).
The state of revulsion toward the object of focus is precisely the path of preparation for detachment (*vairāgyaprayogamārga*).
Second is the attention of counteracting (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*),
which refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);

it comprises a portion of the attention of "delight in gathering" (*saṃlikhita-sukha*) as well as the attention of "separation" (*viveka-manasikāra*) and the attention of "culmination of application" (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-manasikāra*).
Third is the attention that accords with purification,
which is to say, the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Fourth is the attention that accords with investigation (*paryeṣaṇā-manasikāra*).
This means that the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) is the path of diligence;
it involves looking back at whether afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned.
Furthermore, the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-adhimokṣa*) and a portion of the mental application of delight (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*) are also termed "conformable" (*anuloma*).
The distancing from preparatory application (*prayoga*) and one portion of the "delight in cultivation" (*āsvādana*) is called the "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).
One portion of the "delight in cultivation" is called "conducive to purification" (*viśuddhy-anukūla*).
The "attention consisting of investigation" (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) is called "conducive to investigation" (*mīmāṃsā-anukūla*).
Therefore, the four modes of attention encompass the preceding six modes of attention.
Below this, the four characteristics to be contemplated during the time of correct attention are explained.
Within the characteristic of causal conditions:
Master Jing’s commentary explains:
"The accumulation of the requisites for samādhi" refers to the arising of aspiration through the causal conditions of reflecting upon the requisites for meditative concentration.
Regarding "deeply generating weariness toward phenomena that are to be reviled": [it means]...

One should contemplate the causes and conditions that can obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and thereby give rise to weariness toward them, while thoroughly and discerningly knowing distraction and non-distraction.
When practicing right contemplation, one is able to thoroughly and discerningly know: "Am I now in meditative absorption, or am I distracted?"
The following clarifies the causes for distraction and non-distraction.
"Not being troubled or provoked by others" clarifies the cause for non-distraction.
Or, when a person who has practiced even with great skill knows the causal conditions for distraction: if,
with vipaśyanā as the primary focus, they internally withdraw the mind and subsequently observe the signs of the causal conditions of that extremely intense contemplation.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the initial cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) serves as the causal condition for the subsequent state of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Likewise, one contemplates that the initial cultivation of calm abiding serves as the causal condition for the subsequently arising superior insight.
Master Ji said:
"Whether it be 'created by humans' or 'created by non-humans,' and so forth,
refers precisely to the perception of disordered signs."
This is the meaning of the Dharma Master’s [explanation].
Furthermore, upon examining the preceding and following passages, it is not so;
for in the sections on "separation from the middle" (*madhyamā-viveka*), it is stated in all cases that [the state] arises by way of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, one should know that these conditions are precisely the conditions for the arising of greed and the like.
Thus, the subsequent passages all state "due to causes and conditions," or "produced by effort."
This arises from the distraction caused by that preparatory application.
If vipaśyanā is weak and clarity is not present, it is due to the causal conditions for distraction;
as for the characteristics of the subsequent causal conditions of extremely intense contemplation:
One should immediately cultivate and accumulate the provisions;
the causes and conditions for their subsequent fulfillment should be understood by analogy from the section on the lower dhyānas within the "Characteristics to be Avoided."
The sign of sinking refers to when,
by relying excessively on calm abiding (*śamatha*),
one contemplates a concordant image and causes the mind to become dull and inferior.
The characteristic of restlessness (*auddhatya*) refers to being excessively dependent upon the aspect of contemplation regarding causal signs,
whereby one contemplates mental images and causes the mind to become uplifted.
"Attachment to signs" refers to when,
regarding the signs of the images within the objective conditions,
one gives rise to craving and attachment, being unable to feel revulsion toward them and instead developing deep defiled clinging.
Regarding the characteristic of distraction:
it refers to when, upon perceiving the signs of those images, humans, non-humans, and so forth cause affliction and provocation therein,
such that the mind wanders outwardly.
These various signs are as previously explained among the thirty-two signs in the *Samāhitabhūmi*.
The signs to be abandoned have already been explained in detail in the preceding *Samāhitabhūmi*.
Therefore, it is not explained in detail here.
Below, it clarifies that through mental attention (*manasikāra*), one gives rise to nine types of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding objects;
furthermore, it explains the "resolute conviction of the mind's understanding" (*manojalpa-adhimokṣa*) concerning limited objects of focus.
According to the concluding text of the lower [section], it says: "Because its objects of perception are narrow and few, this refers to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
If it is called 'vast' in terms of objects of perception, it refers to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
'Immeasurable' refers to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)."
Regarding the tenth [section], the "Explanation of the Functions of Yoga," Master Jìng explains:

This consists of the paths of preparation, immediate succession, liberation, and so forth, which are free from the afflictions of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
"One whose mind is not well-liberated" refers to the obstructions.
Regarding these fourteen mental states that arise while abiding in the causal state,
they arise when one enters the causal conditions for abiding in meditative concentration;
this text provides a general explanation.
Regarding the statement that there are eight types of minds and so forth arising when abiding in the stage of the "Pure Canopy" (*vimalāvaraṇa-bhūmi*):
among these eight, four are remedial factors subsumed under the "not-yet-reached concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Because they can bring about freedom from the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), this stage is called the "Pure Canopy Stage."
Regarding the statement that there are six types of minds arising when abiding in the stage of purification from afflictions:
three of these are the remedies,
which are capable of counteracting the afflictions of the form realm and the formless realm.
As analyzed previously,
Tai states:
"Among the fourteen moments of mind, the first eight are the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) of meditative concentration."
The first [six] arise when one abides in meditative concentration (samādhi) based on the purification of the hindrances through suppression;
the latter six arise when one abides in meditative concentration based on the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*). Ki says:
Regarding "based on the stage of the purified covering" (*viśuddhacchādana-bhūmi*) and so forth:
herein, the fourteen moments of mind during the period of abiding are explained.
When one has not yet attained the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) but abides within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), it is called the stage of the purified covering.
One gives rise to eight kinds of minds;
relying on the uninterrupted path of meditative concentration,
one abandons the afflictions and gives rise to those six minds.
Question: Why are the first eight called "purifying the hindrances" (*viśuddhi-āvaraṇa*), being the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of concentration but not the immediate paths (*ānantarya-mārga*),
whereas the latter six are called "purifying" (*viśuddhi*), being either the concentration itself or the single immediate path?
The commentary states:
For instance, greed, hatred, and delusion are the afflictions to be remedied, while non-greed,
subduing [hatred], and so forth are the remedies that counteract them.
Thus, the six directions are taken as the three objects of governance, which are precisely the three obscurations (*trivaraṇa*).
This refers to the time of movement;
the following eight types refer to the time of abiding.
Whether it be contraction or distraction—
contraction refers to the sign of cessation (śamatha), while distraction refers to mental scattering—
or whether it be sinking or uplifting.
"Laxity" refers to dullness; "exaltation" refers to the sign of uplifting.
If there is agitation, it is precisely restlessness;
if there is non-quiescence, it is non-quiescence.
That is to say, "bad conduct" (*kaukṛtya*) is called non-tranquility (*aśānti*), while "good conduct" (*sukṛta*) is called tranquility (*śānti*).
Furthermore, doubt is non-tranquility, while certainty is tranquility.
Moreover, the path that can eliminate the aforementioned [states] when combined with them is called tranquility.
Combining what has been previously treated as "non-quiescence," this constitutes the individual antidotes known as the stage for purifying the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The hindrances refer specifically to the five hindrances.
Regarding the latter eighteen types in their general characteristics,
there are no distinct objects of abandonment for each.
However, during the latter six stages, it is essential that one first purify all the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) before being able to enter the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*).
If that is so, then the object to be remedied and its remedy must necessarily be simultaneous.
Why, then, is the "preparatory path" (prayoga-mārga) considered the "path of preparation" and the "uninterrupted path" (ānantarya-mārga) considered the "uninterrupted path"?
The meaning is as follows:
Furthermore, as in the previous case of the antidotes such as tranquility (*śamatha*) and so forth:
if the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) suppresses the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) but does not permanently sever them,
then the time when those preceding antidotes suppress [them] constitutes the path of preparation.
That which is to be abandoned is severed by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) simultaneously with it,
because the antidote must arise only when that which is to be abandoned has ceased.
As the treatise says:
Once liberation has been attained, one enters the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*).
Within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), the non-concentrated mind (*avyākṛtacitta*) is precisely that which is to be countered,
because the first eight [stages] each have their own specific antidote.
The path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) involves the analytical contemplation of the mind;
subsequently, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) involves the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, it is called the "path of immediate succession."
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that these clarify the skillful means.

Of the eight mental factors preceding the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), those to be remedied are specifically the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), each having its own distinct object of remedy;
the latter six kinds do not separately eliminate the hindrances, but rather sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) in their entirety.
Thus, one should distinguish this sequence of immediate succession regarding these skillful means;
eight [of them] merely suppress the afflictions and do not constitute their immediate cessation.
Furthermore, within the internal section on the characteristics of the Dharma for those with inferior understanding who possess hindrances:
First, one thoroughly understands the presence or absence of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned.
Next, one thoroughly understands the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) which serve as the antidotes;

since these are all objects of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), only the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is an object of the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*), not an object of the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
"We have come together for this reason.
If one can thus know all the various defiled dharmas as they truly are," Jing said.
One who thoroughly knows all defiled phenomena is able to know the presence or absence of hindrances and fetters,
as well as their intrinsic nature, causes and conditions, disadvantages, and remedies.
Regarding the preceding statement that the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*),
which serve as the remedies, constitute the essence of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*):
this means that knowing the remedies for the aforementioned obstacles constitutes the essence of the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Master Ji said:
"Examining the preceding text, there is no separate explanation for these four types.
They possess only their own nature, their defects, and their remedies; there are no distinct causes and conditions."
If one follows the previous citation where the objects to be remedied, such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), are termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*),
then according to what was stated previously— that understanding the eye-sphere (*cakṣur-āyatana*) as having the fault of bondage is termed "disadvantage" (*ādīnava*)—
the path that remedies this is termed the "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, there is no separate location for the causes and conditions of liberation; if the meaning is not otherwise obstructed, it is as follows:
during the six modes of conduct, the three unwholesome roots are called the causes and conditions of the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is from these causes and conditions that the various afflictions arise.
Furthermore, the seeds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) themselves are called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Moreover, when intrinsic nature arises depending upon a certain location and a certain object, that location is called the causal condition.
Furthermore, the locations such as the eye, which give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) based on the eye up to mental attention (*manasikāra*), are called the causal conditions.
As explained in the exposition of the mindfulness of the body for those of inferior capacity— which clarifies the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena—
so too should mindfulness and abiding be understood.
Thus concludes the first section, which establishes the essential nature [of the foundations of mindfulness].
From here below is the second section, explaining the differences between internal and external applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
First, three questions are posed;
subsequently, they are answered.
In the response, the first section explains the three contemplations through six successive points, followed by a conclusion that clarifies their brevity.
As for the question, "How does one dwell upon the internal body and so forth, cultivating the contemplation of the body and so forth? [the answer follows].
By mentioning "the internal body" and so forth, one includes the internal feelings, mind, and phenomena;
the other two [categories] are to be understood accordingly.
This is explained within the six successive responses.
The initial statement says that if one takes as an object another sentient being external to oneself, it is called "internal-external":
it is termed "internal" because it belongs to the category of sentient beings,
and it is termed "external" because it is not the physical form of one's own body.
Master Ji’s commentary explains:
herein, the middle [level of] object-condition takes both the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived matter (bhautika) as its object without distinction;
whereas the lower fourth [level] takes only the primary elements and not the derived matter, and is thus distinct.

The second [alternative] states: if one takes as an object the five sense faculties—whether belonging to oneself or another—which are appropriated matter, it is called "taking the internal body as an object";
if one takes as an object external matter that is not a faculty and is non-appropriated, it is called "taking the external body as an object."

If one takes as an object the appropriated matter of the five sense-objects that support the faculties—whether belonging to oneself or others—it is called "contemplating the internal and external body" and so forth.
Third, if one takes as an object the matter associated with pliancy within one's own internal meditative absorption, it is called "dwelling in contemplation of the internal body."
The practitioner’s body, though still within the desire realm, is free from coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) due to the attainment of meditative concentration;
this body is thus accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Because one takes this form as an object, it is called "dwelling within the internal body."
Furthermore, one may be designated as "born in the form realm" based on the body being accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
If one takes as an object both another's pliancy and the matter (*rūpa*) that is accompanied by the heavy residues (*dausthulya*),
this is called "abiding within" when taking as an object the matter accompanied by another's pliancy.
That which takes as its object matter associated with the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of others is called "abiding externally.

Within the fourth [dhyāna], that which takes as its object the derived matter of the sense faculties and their objects produced by the four great elements, whether internal or external, is called "abiding both internally and externally."
Regarding the fifth [meditation object], Master Jingshi explains:
if one takes as an object a body with consciousness that has not yet died, it is called "abiding within the body";

if one takes as an object a body belonging to the category of sentient beings that has already died and lacks consciousness—such as in stages like the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*)—it is called "abiding outside the body."

If one takes as an object the present corpse—the physical form of a body devoid of consciousness—and considers that at the preceding moment of its past state before death it possessed the nature of consciousness and was a physical form with consciousness, this is called "abiding internally.

Furthermore, if one takes as an object the present corpse and considers its continuity of type such that in the future it will lack the nature of consciousness, being of a similar dharma-nature and equal dharma-nature, this is called "abiding externally."
To contemplate both ends together is called "dwelling in the internal and external body.
To be equal with external dharmas is called "the nature of equality.
Master Tai said:
If one takes as an object the present corpse—a body of form devoid of consciousness—this is called "external.

This same present corpse, when it was in the past before death and possessed the nature of consciousness, is now, despite lacking consciousness, similar to and equal with its former state of possessing consciousness; thus, it is called "internal."
If one takes as an object the material form of the conscious body that exists in the present and has not yet died, it is called "internal.
This same material form, when it will inevitably die in the future and be devoid of consciousness, is called "external.
This can be understood by analogy with what preceded.
Master Ki further stated:
"The intent here is to clarify that when one sees a corpse, at the time when it formerly possessed consciousness in a past life, this currently manifest corpse is termed 'external';
at the time when it shall possess consciousness again, it is termed 'internal'."
Conditioned by the present body with consciousness, there is the future body without consciousness; it is likewise for the internal and external.
This is because the present body with consciousness and the future body without consciousness share a similar dharma-nature and an equal dharma-nature, being of one mark and without distinction.
The same applies even to the past.
Regarding the sixth [section], the Tripiṭaka Master says:
"This passage appears to refer to the external characteristics of one's own corpse as the 'internal body of external appearance' (*adhyātma-bāhya-kāya*)."
The external appearance of another's corpse is called the "external body.
Jing says:
that which is within the body is called the "middle body."
Furthermore, taking the internal body of another as the "middle body," it is "external" in relation to oneself.
Tai says:
If one takes as an object the external physical forms of one's own internal body that have undergone or not undergone transformations such as bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*),
and also takes as an object the transformed or untransformed physical forms of other bodies,
it is therefore called "internal and external."
Master Ji said:
"If one takes the 'middle body' as its own object, then that which is within one's own internal body is called the 'middle body';
it is precisely the middle body within one's own interior."
These six rounds of explaining the internal and external correspond to seven of the fourteen pairs mentioned previously; that is to say,
the first is the pair of internal and external.
Second is the pair of faculties and non-faculties;
third is the pair of pliancy and heaviness;
fourth is the pair of the agent and the object produced.
Fifth is the pair of existence and non-existence consciousnesses.
Sixth is the pair of the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as the pair of the mutable and the immutable.
The following concludes by showing their scarcity.
This means that because each of the preceding fourteen pairs and so forth also functions through the three types of contemplation according to their respective applications, there are many varieties;
for now, however, we shall clarify the distinctions among seven pairs within this context.
Therefore, it is said that they are few.
Third, the explanation of the purpose for establishing the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
the four applications of mindfulness are established in order to counteract the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
The text consists of four sections:
the first two refute attachments,
while the latter two directly reveal the Dharma.
Regarding the "four paths of tranquility" (*catasraḥ śivapathikāḥ*):
Jingyun states that these are the tranquil paths in the four directions.
Baizhang said:
"There are four kinds of greed.
First, greed for visible color."
Second, greed for shape; third, greed for service;
fourth, greed for exquisite touch.
One practices the contemplation of impurity regarding these four types of greed.
Therefore, the contemplation of impurity also has four paths:
namely, the path of desolation in a charnel ground, which is silent and devoid of people;
and that which consists of knowing, as they truly are, the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates one conceives of, thereby severing the inversion of self.

To know that the various aggregates (skandhas) consist solely of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), each being distinct and entirely devoid of a self (ātman), is called "knowing their specific characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa).
To know that all aggregates are equally without self is called "knowing their common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, the inversion of self is eliminated.
If explained in detail, each of the four—body and so forth—has its own four [inversions].
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
Although each of these four dharmas has four aspects,
one should primarily contemplate the body as impure and feelings as suffering.
The mind predominantly contemplates impermanence,
while phenomena predominantly contemplate selflessness.
Regarding the second stage, it is because one experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth by depending on the body.
It is because of the self that one experiences pleasure and pain based on the body;
furthermore, one clings to the self as the experiencer of pleasure and pain;
and moreover, it is by means of the mind that one can give rise to defilement or purification regarding what is dharma and what is non-dharma.
Master Ji says:
Regarding those who experience suffering and pleasure,
it is as stated in the "Explanation of the Lower Covering" (Xiàfù jiè zhōng yún):

For the fool who clings to a self in the mind, consciousness, and mentation, the application of mindfulness to the mind is established because of his delusion regarding the objective basis of the self (*ātman-vastu*);
that is, he conceives of this very mind as being the self.
This is the opposite of the first [application of mindfulness].
Regarding the third section: it refers to the body upon which one relies to create karma;
the purpose for which one creates karma;
and the agent who creates karma—that is, one who creates karma by means of wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.
The subsequent text is to be understood accordingly.
Regarding the fourth section: it refers to whether defilement and purity exist in dependence upon this body, or whether defilement and purity arise for the sake of this feeling.
If the mind is the master of defilement and purification, then it should be understood that defilement and purification are established by virtue of various phenomena.
This is the fourth general explanation of the meaning of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
If one maintains mindfulness while abiding in this, it is called the foundation of mindfulness as the object (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna).
Because one dwells with established mindfulness upon these objects—body, feeling, mind, and phenomena—it is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
By virtue of this dwelling in mindfulness, it is even the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Because this wisdom and mindfulness sustain meditative concentration, it is said that "one dwells in mindfulness by means of this.
Both mindfulness and wisdom are its intrinsic nature;
the essence of the foundations of mindfulness is the same as that described in the Abhidharma.

The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* differs [from other treatises] in that it maintains that wisdom (*prajñā*) alone is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement "arising through the predominance of body, feeling, mind,

and phenomena," although the essence of wisdom and mindfulness have previously been analyzed as the essential nature of the foundations of mindfulness, [this passage clarifies their specific modes of arising].
Since it was not yet known what kind of wisdom this "wisdom" is,
it is brought forth here:
all three types of wisdom arising with the body and so forth as their object— whether they be tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*)— are applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
